items.text:
Running a Raspberry Pi or another SBC? OpenCreator for SBC runs the same stack there, with the printer's boards tunnelled over USB. Want to stay close to stock? OpenCreator Legacy works around FlashForge's software instead of replacing it.

Warranty and responsibility

items.title: OpenCreator
items.text:
Open-source custom firmware for the FlashForge Creator 5 and Creator 5 Pro.

Kalico (Klipper) on the printer, a real toolchanger you control, AFC filament handling and Fluidd or Mainsail, all on the hardware you already own. Every part is open source and can be changed.

Get started Latest release Discord How we're different

items.title: Why OpenCreator?
items.text:
• Kalico on the printer

    A Klipper fork with MPC heater tuning, input shaper graphs drawn on the printer, power loss recovery and timelapse.

  • A real Klipper toolchanger

    Switch heads with T0–T3 with no extra software, load several tools in one go, and calibrate one nozzle without redoing all four. See how fast it changes

  • Filament that knows itself

    AFC with toolchanger support, ACE Pro auto feed and load, and material and colour synced into OrcaSlicer like an AMS.

  • Fluidd, Mainsail and GrumpyScreen

    Full web control, so the touchscreen is optional. A faster camera stream, SFTP and 3MF uploads come with it.

  • Open and editable

    Plain Klipper configs, toggles for every behaviour and a plugin system. Every repository is on GitHub.

  • Active community

    Developers and Creator 5 owners in one place, for help, testing and what's next. Join the Discord

items.title: Pick your edition
items.text:
• OpenCreator CFW

    Replaces FlashForge's software with Kalico, Moonraker and a web UI on the printer's own computer. The full feature set.

  • OpenCreator for SBC

    The same stack on a Raspberry Pi or other SBC, for more speed and room than the printer's MIPS board.

  • OpenCreator Legacy

    Keeps the stock experience and adds comforts like a better camera. A slight change that really doesn't do much.

Development software

Don't treat any full custom firmware from us as complete. What you've seen from reviews, videos, or anything related outside of this wiki may be out of date, different, or not working.

Not sure which one? Is OpenCreator CFW for you? walks through what you gain and what you give up. The feature list and status and roadmap show what's finished and what's still in testing.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
The full custom firmware effort has layers (like an onion!) The printer's Linux host runs Klipper and web services. Four MCU boards perform motion, extrusion, heating, and sensing. AFC models the removable tools and filament state. Printer-side configuration ties those parts together.

Layer Current development role Source Linux host Runs Kalico (the Creator 5 Klipper fork), Moonraker, and the configured web interface. The printer is MIPS32 (Ingenic X2600 / Xburst 2 with 512MB of RAM) kalico Mainboard MCU Handles the main motion and machine I/O through the GD32 port. Chip is a gd32h737vgt6. Also uses a "MCLib" motion library for complex stuff like VFA compensation. kalico/src/c5_mainboardgd.c, c5_mclib.c and related target code, klippy/extras/mclib.py eboard MCU Drives the shared physical extruder motor and supplies the pressure-advance measurement interface. Chip is n32g455ccl7. kalico/src/c5_eboard.c, c5_eboard_pa.c and klippy/extras/pa_adjust.py Heaterboard MCU Handles tool heater and temperature I/O. Chip is n32g455rel7. kalico/src/stm32 N32G45x support (C5_HEATERBOARD build option) Levelboard MCU Supplies probe and levelboard-specific sensing used by calibration. Chip is n32g430f8s7. kalico/src/c5_levelboard.c and Klippy levelboard code Toolchanger and AFC Uses physical dock and grab inputs for T0 to T3 selection. AFC standalone provides filament and tool mapping, while creator5_toolchanger.py owns the machine-specific motion and safety checks. kalico/klippy/extras Printer filesystem Holds the Creator 5 configuration, AFC configuration, scripts, and printer data layout. opencreator-fs

items.title: Printer-side layout
items.text:
The SoC configuration is organized below /usr/data/opencreator/klipper/configs on the printer. printer.base.cfg includes the Creator 5, probe, motor, filament, vibration, Misc, and AFC files. G-code storage is configured at /usr/data/gcodes. Stock-format calibration data remains under /usr/data/firmwareRes/config, including extruder.json, zoffset.json, and test.json.

The Creator 5 has no chamber heater, chamber fans or aux fan, so those are in printer.pro.cfg. They're only included on a Creator 5 Pro, through printer.model.cfg. On the printer, that file is written at every boot, from the model in the stock boot script (MACHINE= in /usr/prog/app_startup.sh). In tunnel mode, the Pi installer asks which printer it's connected to. On a Creator 5, M106/M107 P2 and P3 do nothing, and M191 says there's no chamber heater instead of failing.

The config layout is originally based on FlashForge's default config layout, just expanded with new macros, settings, and removals of useless settings. This does not mean our config is interchangable with stock firmware, and if you try, it will not work as a lot of settings are intertwined with our Kalico.

There is one physical extrusion motor. The four Klipper extruder contexts select the corresponding tool heaters and state; they are not four independent extrusion drives. A toolchange must agree with the dock and grab pins before the selected logical extruder becomes active.

The single motor driver is configured on the eBoard as identical [tmc2209 extruder] through [tmc2209 extruder3] sections, one for each logical extruder for CFW. See MCU development and verification for pin assignments.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text: The printer configuration currently uses AFC standalone mode, not a BoxTurtle or AMS-like mechanism. Mainsail/Fluidd exposes virtual Misc switches for flow calibration and purge. GrumpyScreen work is separate from the core Klipper and filesystem repositories, and is mostly kept up to date and commited to mainline SimpleAF GrumpyScreen.

items.title: Hardware
items.text:
Other than the previously explained hardware for the MCU chips, the printer has some unexplained "maximum" limits for temperature

Hardware Default Max Actual Max Safe Max Nozzles 320c 350c 350c? Chamber Heater (Pro) 65c 80c 70c? Bed 120 130 125?

Safe Max temps are the maximium safe temperatures before you run into actual hardware limitations. Anything with a ? may mean untested.

Known hardware limitations

  • Above 70 degrees chamber temperature, the grill will deform
  • Above 320 degrees, the nozzle may start recording wildly off temperatures

items.title: Research and inspiration
items.text:
Work we learned from without using its code:

  • Prusa Research, phase stepping (blog post, help article, Prusa-Firmware-Buddy, GPLv3). Their finding that each stepper motor has its own ripple, and that a per-motor correction calibrated with the toolhead accelerometer on diagonal moves can cancel most of it, is the idea behind Quieter motors. Our version runs on the Creator 5's own motor control (MCLib) rather than Trinamic drivers, keeps Klipper's steps, and calibrates a correction per speed; see that page for how it differs.

items.title: There were both human and AI use.
OpenCreator CFW Full Feature Set
items.text:
Finished works on a printer   Semi-Finished partly done   Testing in testing or untested   Broken not working yet

Feature Implementation Description ZMax on Print End Finished Puts the bed to the very bottom of the build area, for easy grabbing, a suggestion from @josemyab Allow for near zero purge printing Finished You can turn off purge and flow calibration to have almost zero purge on start, a half suggestion from @josemyab Purge line toggle Testing The purge line in front of the print has its own purge_line switch (on by default), separate from the bucket purge; see How to toggle features. Chamber heats with the bed (Pro Only) Testing Print start turns the chamber heater on together with the bed, without waiting for it, using the chamber temperature from the slicer's filament settings. Allow for calibration of only one toolhead Finished You don't need to calibrate all offsets to update z-offset of a nozzle, for switching nozzles. Saved baby stepping per tool Testing Baby stepping Z during a print is saved to that tool's Z offset, so the next print starts from it. LIST_BABYSTEP shows each tool's value and CLEAR_BABYSTEP TOOL= resets one or all; see Baby stepping. Allow for configuration of nozzle calibration Finished If your nozzle doesn't fit the min mm for levelboard, you can set it higher. Filament runout and switchover support Untested Give a tool a backup in AFC ("Infinite Spool") and a runout switches to it by itself, with the run-out tool's Tx commands sent to the backup. With no backup, it pauses and asks: switch to another loaded tool, or load new filament. AFC Toolchanger Finished Allows for the use of AFC filament system, but with toolchangers. Should be fully functional except for "loaded" filament buttons. GrumpyScreen Toolchanger Support Semi-Finished GrumpyScreen now properly shows all extruders and currently in use extruder, but you cannot extrude yet. Stock Feature Parity Finished Should have feature parity. Every FlashForge firmware version Finished Installs on any FlashForge release, 1.7.8 up to the latest 2.0.0 (kernel 2.0.8), with no need to update or downgrade first. See Supported FlashForge firmware. Full WebUI support Finished You can avoid using the touchscreen, and don't even need it in general. SFTP over SSH Finished Transfer and manage files over SSH using SFTP, unlike stock firmware, which requires SCP for file transfers. Automatic Fan control for Heated Chamber (Pro Only) Finished Removes user fan control, and makes it automatically turn on when the chamber is set to something. Make Camera Better / Faster Finished Uses pre-installed MJPEG streamer over stock camera control in the touchscreen executable, making it efficient and fast. Input shaper graphs Finished CALIBRATE_INPUT_SHAPER_GRAPH calibrates input shaper and draws Klipper's frequency response graph for each axis on the printer itself, no PC needed; see Input shaper graphs. Timelapse Finished Moonraker Timelapse records a frame per layer from the printer camera and renders the video when the print ends; see Timelapse. Installed by the OpenCreator Installer. VDS filament dryer (SoC) Finished Start, stop and pause FlashForge's two-chamber dryer from Fluidd or macros, with each chamber graphed as a temperature sensor; see Filament dryer. Allow to switch toolheads arbitraily Finished You can send commands T0-T3 or click the buttons to pick up the toolheads. Allow to load multiple toolheads simultaneously Finished You can send the load command for multiple tools, which changes them, loads, then docks. Allow for reading colour information and material information on Orca Finished OrcaSlicer syncs the filament list from the printer like an AMS: material and colour for every tool. Needs a current OrcaSlicer development build. ACE Pro auto feed and auto load Finished Each ACE slot feeds its own head. A new spool is fed to the head's filament sensor by itself, and pressing load takes it into the gears and purges. Feeds made during a print wait until it ends. ACE Pro multiplexing Planned Several ACE slots feeding one head, in the planning stages. Raspberry Pi Host support Finished Allowing to use a Raspberry Pi over the stock MIPS32 CPU, by tunneling the MCUs through the SoC through gadget mode USBs. Power Loss Recovery Finished Allows to resume a print from power loss or MCU errors. The resumed print keeps its bed mesh, layer count, print time and estimates. Until you resume or discard it, the bed is kept at the print's temperature so the part stays stuck down; discarding turns the heaters off. Kalico Support Finished On all installs, you install Kalico, a beefed up Klipper fork with features such as MPC tuning. Removal of FlashForge services Finished You can completely disable FlashForge's things, and make it like it never existed. Full Orcaslicer with Moonraker Agent. Filament sync Finished Syncs your filaments (material and colour) into OrcaSlicer. Needs a current OrcaSlicer development build; older releases had a bug that broke it. Turn off cooling fan when chamber heater is on Finished It will actively say in console that it has been turned off, making it where cold air won't mess with the heated chamber Bed warp stabilization (bed soak) Finished Optionally waits at bed temperature for a configurable number of minutes immediately before a fresh mesh, letting the plate finish warping/expanding so the mesh reflects its settled shape instead of its heat-up transient. Skipped when the bed target is below 45 °C. Chamber heat wait toggle Finished Controls whether M191 blocks until the chamber actually reaches target, or just sets the target and lets the print start heating in the background while early layers print (M141-like). Toggle with C5_MISC_CHAMBER_WAIT_ON / OFF. OpenCreator Updater Finished A dedicated Moonraker update_manager entry that merges the latest config template into your live printer_data/config without clobbering values you've customized (speeds, toggle defaults, etc), then pulls Klipper -- all from one "Update" click. Uses a real three-way merge, so a conflicting change is left for you to resolve by hand instead of guessed at or silently overwritten. SoC/LoopScript installs get an equivalent boot-time version, not yet verified on real hardware. First-time setup dialog In development After installing, Fluidd, Mainsail and the screen walk you through pressure advance calibration, purging, Clog Detection and bed heat soak, point out the calibrations worth running (VFA on the printer; offsets, input shaper and VFA on an SBC), then point you to the Discord. Input shaper and PID come from FlashForge's calibration, imported on a first install. Shown until finished once; C5_FIRST_SETUP shows it again. 3MF uploads Finished Upload a sliced .gcode.3mf from OrcaSlicer or Bambu Studio straight to Fluidd or from the slicer; the first sliced plate is extracted with its thumbnail. SBC installs. OpenCreator Fluidd theme Finished An extra-dark Fluidd theme with the OpenCreator logo. Installed and updated with the config. Updater self-repair Untested repair.sh fixes "No git repo detected" in the update manager: starts git where it is missing, syncs to the official main branch, fixes moonraker.conf. Door open notification Finished With C5_MISC_DOOR_NOTIFY_ON (or the door_notify switch in Fans & Outputs), opening the top or front door during a print, or starting a print with one open, shows an error pop-up in Fluidd and Mainsail and beeps (unless quiet mode is on). Uncomment [notifier door_open] in moonraker.conf to also get it on your phone. C5_DOORS shows whether each door is open. Chamber fan follows the heater Finished The chamber heater fan turns off as soon as the chamber heater's target is cleared, instead of running until the chamber cools below 50 °C. Chamber heater fan full speed toggle (Pro Only) Finished The chamber heater fan normally slows to half speed once the chamber is near its target. Turn on chamber_heat_fan_full in Fans & Outputs (or C5_MISC_CHAMBER_HEAT_FAN_FULL_ON / OFF) to keep it at 90% whenever the chamber heater is on. The setting survives restarts. Wi-Fi beep fallback Finished (Pi-tunnel) If a board is pinned to 4 tunnel ports (no dedicated beep serial channel), C5_BUZZER can fall back to sending the beep request over the network to the tunnel bridge instead of silently going quiet. Opt-in via network_host in [creator5_remote_beeper]. Quieter motors Testing The mainboard follows the real move between steps and cancels each X/Y motor's own wobble, calibrated with RIPPLE_CALIBRATE. Up to 40–60% less toolhead vibration at printing speeds; see Quieter motors. Needs the phase-stepping mainboard firmware. Quieter board fans Finished The mainboard and power supply fans ramp with the board's temperature and the power supply's load instead of running at full speed whenever the printer is busy; see Mainboard and power supply fans. MCU temperatures Finished The mainboard and toolhead board chips' temperatures show in Fluidd and Mainsail; see MCU temperatures. Motion guard Testing Skipped step and stall detection for X, Y and Z, off by default; see Motion guard. VDS Support Finished VDS Support is available, but untested as no one on the development team owns a VDS or plans on owning a VDS.

items.title: Contributing documentation
items.text:
Edit pages under docs/ and add new pages to nav in mkdocs.yml. For hardware instructions, say which printer model, firmware version and source commit they're for, and how they were tested. Say plainly when something hasn't been tested.

Make sure to use clear language and only delve into techincal specs and docs on parts where it would be expected.

Before proposing a change, build the site with warnings treated as errors:

.venv/bin/python -m zensical build --strict

On Windows, use .venv\Scripts\python.exe. The generated site/ directory is ignored by Git; only the source Markdown and configuration should be committed.

items.title: Videos and other raw HTML
items.text: Markdown images and links work with relative paths. Paths inside raw HTML, such as <video> or <source src="...">, don't: the site loads pages without a full reload, and a relative src is then resolved against the page you came from. Give media in raw HTML its full URL, for example https://opencreatorcfw.github.io/assets/videos/<file>.mp4.

items.title: The difference with OpenCreator
items.text:
There's a plethora of mods now for the Creator 5, what makes us different?

It's not special that there's a couple mods apart from us now. Even though we were first on the scene with our stock mods, doesn't mean we stopped innovating when others came out with their solutions.

items.title: Features
items.text:
We're the first to fully reverse all MCU code and thus, can improve certain features with it such as allowing for double stepping on the extruder motor, having completely addressable TMC2209s instead of hardcoding. Due to it no longer being hardcoded, you can now adjust motor current on the fly for the extruder.

This also makes our firmware completely incompatible with stock and other mods that piggy back off of the stock firmware which is all at the time of writing.

We're also currently the only custom firmware that has this.

We also actively take in suggestions.

We also have Power Loss Recovery, which isn't a given as most CFWs made do not have fully implemented PLR. On power loss, it will prompt you to restart your print, and will keep the bed warmed, so even if you aren't there, your print can be saved.

items.title: Up to 2x faster toolchanges
items.text:
A stock toolchange usually takes about 6 seconds. On OpenCreator CFW one can take as little as 3 seconds, so multi-color and multi-material prints spend far less time swapping tools.

Watch the toolchange video

items.title: Better timelapses
items.text:
OpenCreator CFW takes a camera frame at every layer change and turns them into a smooth MP4 when the print finishes, using Moonraker Timelapse. The videos are under Timelapse in Fluidd and Mainsail, where you can also change the frame rate or park the toolhead for each frame.

Watch the timelapse

items.title: Fixes stock firmware bugs
items.text: FlashForge's firmware has a bug where switching extruders whilst one is unloading can make the extruder run backwards. OpenCreator CFW fixes this.

items.title: Klipper
items.text: We're fully Kalico, a fork of Klipper with more features. No FlashForge, no old Klipper.

items.title: Different hosts
items.text: You're not forced to cope with a bad SoC with the printer, just plug in a new host like a Raspberry Pi, and get to printing!

items.title: Support over Discord
items.text: Unlike others, we have a centralized Discord where we take feedback and support people. Check it out on the landing page.

items.title: Support for stock installs
items.text: If you really don't want to break too much of your warranty, you can stick with OpenCreator Legacy, where we only modify a little bit, and keep things mostly stock, FlashForge services and all.

items.title: Maintainable Source
items.text: Unlike some other mods, our source code is easily readable and is reasonably split up on the repository, making it very easy to understand what we do.

items.title: Mainstream UIs
items.text: Most of our UIs and backends such as Mainsail and Fluidd, along with Moonraker are mainstream, not forked, and only come with a CSS theme, update as soon as updates come out.

items.title: Up to 3x* better performance
items.text:
With our custom compiled special ingredients that we sprinkle into our custom firmware, you are less likely to ever run into a Timer Too Close, or Motor Too Far In The Past, and can run a print without a purge tower without the printer crashing.

(* - 3x best case scenario, most of the time from 1.5 to 2x from completely stock 1.9.9)

items.title: No slowed-down short moves
items.text:
Since 1.9.9, stock firmware avoids Timer Too Close by slowing down short moves, whether your print needed it or not:

  • Every move of 0.75 mm or less is slowed so it takes at least 2.5 ms. A 0.2 mm move can go no faster than 80 mm/s, however fast the slicer asked for.
  • Any short move that extrudes (0.75 mm or less across) is capped at 80 mm/s.
  • On top of that, the motion planner limits acceleration on them. In 1.9.9, always: short moves to 5000 mm/s², and short extruding moves to 80 mm/s at 1500 mm/s². In 2.0.0, moves of 0.3 mm or less are limited to 10000 mm/s², and extruding moves of 0.5 mm or less to 120 mm/s at 5000 mm/s². That applies when moves come in faster than 80 a second (fully from 200), and for the first 100 moves of a print.

Curves, arcs, small details and fine infill are made of exactly these short moves, so stock prints them slower than the slicer planned for.

OpenCreator CFW has none of these limits: every move runs at the speed in your G-code. We keep up with the moves instead of slowing them down (see above).

items.title: Full installer
items.text: Instead of picking afterwards, or not being able to pick at all, our installer environment will allow you to pick what you like, before it even installs, and if your printer breaks but can still access USB drives, you can use our installer to fix any problems, over SSH.

items.title: Better VFA compensation
items.text:
FlashForge keeps a lot of their special sauce for their VFA calibration disabled. We fix up their disabled options and make it better.

Read the wiki page on VFA Compensation

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
OpenCreator has two paths. Legacy keeps the mostly stock FlashForge control stack and adds selected modifications. OpenCreator CFW replaces more of that stack with community-maintained Klipper and printer-side components. CFW is in public alpha: download the latest release and see Installation and safety.

If you want to improve a stock printer today, start with the Creator-5-Mods Legacy guides. Follow the prerequisites for each individual modification.

If you are contributing to CFW, start with Project layout and Architecture. The printer configuration lives in opencreator-fs/fs/usr/data/config, while the Creator 5 Klipper modules and MCU code live in kalico. The detailed toolchanger development notes are in CREATOR5_TOOLCHANGER.md inside the configuration tree.

Join our Discord for support and to report problems with the alpha.

items.title: Before installing on a printer
items.text:
• Read Status and roadmap
  • Read Installation and safety
  • Know how to revert to stock firmware
  • Have a USB drive that meets the requirements
  • Join the Discord for support

items.title: Installation and safety
items.text:
OpenCreator CFW is in public alpha. Download the latest release on GitHub.

Alpha

This is an alpha. Expect bugs, keep a backup, and know how to go back to stock. Report problems on the Discord.

CFW is installed with the OpenCreator Installer, a touchscreen app that backs up the printer before changing anything. If you want a mostly stock printer instead, use the Legacy path and its own instructions.

items.title: Supported FlashForge firmware
items.text:
OpenCreator supports every FlashForge firmware version released for the Creator 5 and Creator 5 Pro, from 1.7.8 up to the latest, 2.0.0. You don't need to update or downgrade before installing.

FlashForge firmware Kernel package 1.7.8 to 1.9.7 2.0.1 to 2.0.5 1.9.8 2.0.6 1.9.9 2.0.7 2.0.0 2.0.8

A newer FlashForge release with a new kernel needs an installer update first; until then the installer stops without changing anything. See Supported kernel packages.

items.title: Requirements for USB
items.text:
• FAT32 Partition
  • At least 4GB in size
  • USB is recommended to have at least 8GB for the backup step

items.title: Requirement for printer
items.text:
• A printer that has at least 200MB on the prog partition and 1gb of storage on the data partition
  • A printer that has an active and stable internet connection of at least 1 mbps

items.title: Steps to install OpenCreator
items.text:
1. Download the zip from the latest release and extract it to the root of the USB drive
  2. Reboot the printer with the USB plugged in
  3. Go through the steps, SoC installs are recommended for people who don't know what tunneled is
  4. Wait about 15-30 minutes for things to install (Backing up takes the longest)
  5. After it is finished, it will prompt you to remove the USB drive and press the reboot button
  6. Once you reboot, you should see a new boot logo, and Grumpyscreen, and on the web under the printer IP, Fluidd.
  7. Set up your slicer for OpenCreator: follow Slicer Configuration before your first print.

items.title: Steps to update OpenCreator
items.text: There are two ways.

items.title: Way 1: Fluidd/Mainsail
items.text:
Fluidd and Mainsail have a way for smaller updates that don't effect most packages on the printer.

  1. Navigate to the software update section
  2. Update "OpenCreator" then "Klipper"
  3. Reboot via switch or host restart

items.title: Way 2: OpenCreator Installer Update
items.text:
Sometimes an update can't be distributed like that, this is the other way for more major updates.

  1. Load the update by copying files overtop the existing files
  2. Plug in the USB drive and reboot
  3. Update with backups or without backups (Backups will make it last significantly longer and are not required for updates)
  4. Restart when it prompts you

items.title: Uninstalling OpenCreator
items.text:
To uninstall OpenCreator and go back to bone stock, launch the installer, and follow instructions for a full rollback

Files left over

There are some files left over from uninstalling, they can be removed via /usr/data/opencreator /usr/data/grumpyscreen /usr/data/python-hf Moonraker will also be updated, and will have to be reinstalled if you go back to stock, you'll have to find the download for the old version.

If you uninstall OpenCreator and you picked Fluidd, you'll have to revert Nginx to stock configs.

items.title: Restoring the stock boot logo
items.text:
The OpenCreator boot logo will be removed when you use the full-rollback option. Here's a way if you do it via normal software updates.

  1. Download the stock logo
  2. Copy it over /usr/prog/logo.jpeg on the printer, keeping that file name
  3. Reboot the printer

items.title: OpenCreator Installer
items.text: The OpenCreator Installer is a touchscreen app that runs on the Creator 5's own screen. It walks you through installing OpenCreator CFW from a USB drive: on the printer itself, or tunneled to a Raspberry Pi / SBC. It backs everything up first, so you can go back. Its source is the opencreator-installer repository.

items.title: Download
items.text: The installer is part of each OpenCreator release; use the latest one. Extract the zip to the root of a FAT32 USB drive, then follow Steps to install OpenCreator.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• A Creator 5 or Creator 5 Pro on FlashForge firmware (1.9.9 recommended)
  • A USB drive that meets the requirements
  • Internet on the printer (Entware, Kalico, Moonraker and the web UIs are downloaded during install)
  • For tunnel mode: an SBC, see OpenCreator for SBC
  • A printer that has at least 200MB on the prog partition and 1gb of storage on the data partition

items.title: How it goes
items.text:
flowchart TD
  A[Check printer model<br/>and kernel package] --> B{Supported?}
  B -->|no| S[Stop: nothing is changed]
  B -->|yes| E{Where should<br/>Klipper run?}
  E -->|On printer SoC| F[Choose Fluidd or Mainsail]
  F --> G[Install GrumpyScreen?]
  E -->|Tunneled| G
  G --> H[Ready to install:<br/>summary]
  H --> I[Back up, then install]
  I --> J[Reboot]
  1. Checking. The installer reads the printer model and FlashForge kernel package. The printer's root filesystem is not changed; everything is installed next to the stock software. The bottom of the screen shows the installer version, the MCU firmware on the drive (and what the boards last got, if OpenCreator flashed them before), the kernel package and the build date.

2. Where should Klipper run? On printer SoC installs everything on the printer. Tunneled turns the printer's board into a bridge for an SBC. Both work on every supported FlashForge firmware version. Choosing Tunneled asks for the tunneled-mode password, typed on the screen's keyboard, both for a first install and for switching an installed printer to tunneled. It isn't asked again when the printer is already tunneled.

3. Web interface (SoC only): Fluidd (recommended) or Mainsail. Both are installed; the one you pick is the one the printer's web page shows.

4. Touchscreen: install GrumpyScreen (recommended) or not.

5. Ready to install shows the printer, mode, web UI and touchscreen you chose. Back up and install starts; Install without backup skips the backup (faster when re-running); Demo install does a dry run (below).

6. Installing shows each step live with its number (Step 3 of 11), a progress bar and elapsed time. Installing Entware and the Python packages takes a while.

7. Installation complete: reboot from the button, then unplug the USB drive.

items.title: Already installed
items.text:
If the printer already has OpenCreator from the same installer version, the installer opens on OpenCreator is up to date:

  • Update again re-runs the update with the current setup.
  • Recovery runs the whole setup again, as above.
  • Update Configs asks the same questions (where Klipper runs, web UI, touchscreen), then shows only what differs from the current setup and changes just that. For example, switching from On printer SoC to Tunneled only installs the bridge, and switching back only installs what SoC mode needs and isn't on the printer yet. Switching web UI changes which one the printer serves; turning the touchscreen off keeps GrumpyScreen on the printer but stops starting it. Nothing is backed up. Reboot afterwards.
  • Restore backup and Rollback to stock show up when there's a backup or FlashForge's own firmwareExe to go back to.

items.title: Update available
items.text: With an older OpenCreator installed, it opens on Update available, which updates in place with the setup shown. Your configs and files are kept; OpenCreator files you changed are saved to the backup. Change setup asks the questions again.

items.title: No internet
items.text: Without internet, it lists the Wi-Fi networks it can see. Tap one and type its password on the screen's keyboard. Quit starts the printer normally.

items.title: Clean up storage
items.text:
Every start page (first install, update, already installed, no internet, unsupported kernel) has Clean up storage. Its confirmation page warns that nothing can be brought back, and Yes, delete only works after a 10-second countdown. It deletes:

  • every print file (.gcode, .3mf, .stl), .mp4 and log under /usr/data and /usr/prog;
  • everything in /usr/data/logs, /usr/data/update (FlashForge update downloads), /usr/data/opencreator/timelapse, /usr/data/opencreator/klipper/logs and the Entware caches;
  • other mods' leftovers (ZMOD, Anvil), old Moonraker copies, and the stock Klipper docs and man pages.

Git checkouts (Klipper, Moonraker, opencreator-fs and the rest), the stock firmware's own model files and the installer's backups are kept. It can't be undone, and OpenCreator takes no responsibility for anything it breaks or removes. Based on CleanFlashforgeCreator5Pro.

Supported kernel packages

Entware needs legacy NaN, which is switched on with one byte written at an address that depends on the FlashForge kernel package (/usr/prog/PROGRAM/kernel/): 0x00a130d1 for 2.0.1 to 2.0.6, 0x00B330D1 for 2.0.7 (FlashForge 1.9.9) and 0x00B030D1 for 2.0.8 (FlashForge 2.0.0). On any other package the installer stops without changing anything.

items.title: What gets installed
items.text: On printer SoCTunneled Step What happens Entware The Entware package manager in /usr/data/bin/opt, with git, gcc, Python and Moonraker's build dependencies. LoopScript OpenCreator's startup system from opencreator-fs: it replaces FlashForge's firmwareExe (a copy of the original is kept) and starts everything below at boot. It also replaces the boot logo with the OpenCreator one (the original is backed up). MCU firmware Flashes all four boards (eBoard, heaterBoard, levelBoard, mainBoardGD) from the package on the USB drive, after checking its checksum. Skipped if the boards already run that firmware. Klipper Kalico with the OpenCreator printer config, including the first-time setup dialog and the OpenCreator Fluidd theme, in /usr/data/opencreator/klipper. A first install takes the printer's input shaper and hotend and bed PID tuning from FlashForge's config; a config you already have there is kept. Moonraker The latest Moonraker, replacing FlashForge's older one. Its update manager lists Kalico, Moonraker, Mainsail, Fluidd and opencreator (the OpenCreator configs). Updating opencreator merges the new config templates into yours within a minute, keeping your own edits. Restart Klipper afterwards to load them. Web UI The latest Mainsail and Fluidd; the printer's web page shows the one you chose. Touchscreen The latest GrumpyScreen release, if chosen. Root login Adds the root login opencreator (password FlashForge2026) for SSH. See Root login. Step What happens Entware The Entware package manager, with git, gcc and socat. LoopScript Same as SoC mode; in tunnel mode it starts the bridge instead of Klipper. MCU firmware Same as SoC mode. Bridge Installs the socat bridge and switches the printer's board to bridge-only mode, so it forwards the four boards to your SBC over USB. Touchscreen The latest GrumpyScreen release, if chosen. Point it at your SBC afterwards: set host under [moonraker] in /usr/data/grumpyscreen/grumpyscreen.cfg. Root login Same as SoC mode. SBC Not done by the installer: after rebooting the printer, run the SBC installer from OpenCreator for SBC.

items.title: Root login
items.text:
The installer adds a root login, so you can SSH into the printer:

User opencreator Password FlashForge2026 
ssh opencreator@<printer IP>

Change the password

Everyone who installs OpenCreator gets the same default password. To set your own, log in over SSH and run:

passwd opencreator

Type the new password twice. Running the installer again keeps the password you set.

items.title: Safety features
items.text:
• Model check

    Only a Creator 5 (PID 0028) or Creator 5 Pro (PID 0029) on a supported kernel package is accepted. Otherwise installing is blocked.

  • Backup first

    Before anything changes, FlashForge's firmwareExe, Moonraker, the opencreator folder (Klipper and your config), the web UI folders and the nginx config are archived to the USB drive.

  • Restore

    If a backup exists, the installer offers Restore backup, also right after a failed install. Folders that did not exist before are removed again. MCU firmware is not rolled back, and Entware stays installed.

  • Preflight warnings

    Warns when there is less than 256 MB free on the printer or the USB drive, or the backup folder is missing or read-only.

  • Log

    The Log button shows everything the installer did. The same log is saved to the USB drive as opencreator-installer.log.

  • Demo install

    Runs every step for real, but writes into a separate folder instead of the system, so you can see exactly what would change without touching the printer.

When the install finishes, it records what was installed (installer version, model, mode, web UI, touchscreen, backup location and time) in /usr/data/opencreator/install.json. The next run shows that as the previous install.

Power

Do not power off the printer while the installer is running, especially during MCU flashing. A power loss there can leave the printer needing firmware recovery.

items.title: Is OpenCreator CFW for you?
items.text: OpenCreator CFW replaces FlashForge's software on the Creator 5 and Creator 5 Pro with Kalico, Moonraker and a web UI. It's in public alpha, so it suits some people more than others.

items.title: You'll like CFW if you
items.text:
• Want faster toolchanges

    Up to 2x faster: about 6 seconds on stock, as little as 3 seconds on CFW.

  • Want a full web UI

    Fluidd or Mainsail with Moonraker, straight from the mainstream projects. You don't need the touchscreen at all.

  • Like to tune and tinker

    Kalico with MPC, input shaper graphs on the printer, per-tool Z offsets, toggles for purge, flow calibration, bed soak and more. See CFW Features.

  • Use OrcaSlicer

    Print over the Moonraker agent, with material and colour synced from every tool like an AMS.

  • Want FlashForge's services gone

    You can disable them completely, cloud included.

  • Want to run a Raspberry Pi as host

    Move Klipper onto an SBC for more power and cameras. See OpenCreator for SBC.

  • Want what's coming next

    More is on the way, including more accurate pressure advance tuned to your filament, and stall and skipped step detection (StallGuard-like) on X, Y and Z, to even better VFA testing and compensation.

items.title: CFW may not be for you yet if you
items.text:
• Rely on the stock touchscreen. GrumpyScreen replaces it fully, new UI.
  • Use FlashForge's app, cloud or FlashStudio. These go away once FlashForge's services are gone.
  • Care about your warranty. Installing mods may void it. You can clean up any traces but they still may figure it out.
  • Want official support. You can't ask FlashForge for software support if you're on custom firmware.
  • Have zero prior experience with 3D printing. You're expected to have at least a basic understanding of Klipper.

items.title: Not sure?
items.text: OpenCreator Legacy keeps the mostly stock FlashForge experience, with creature comforts like better camera views. If CFW sounds right, head to Getting started, and ask in the Discord if you have questions.

items.title: MCU development and verification
items.text:
OpenCreator has separate host software, printer configuration, and firmware for four controller boards. They should be fully working as of 19 of October.

Board MCU Primary role MainboardGD GD32H737VGT6 Main motion and machine I/O eBoard N32G455CCL7 Shared extrusion drive and pressure-advance sensing Heaterboard N32G455REL7 Tool heaters and temperature I/O Levelboard N32G430F8S7 Probing and levelboard sensing

The source for the MCU ports and the host is in kalico. It replaces klipper-c5, which is archived and kept for reference only. The configuration is maintained separately in opencreator-fs and opencreator-tunnel.

items.title: One motor, four logical tools
items.text:
T0 through T3 represent four removable toolheads, but they share one physical extruder motor and its eBoard TMC2209 driver. The logical extruders share the eBoard step, direction, and enable signals. Tool selection associates that drive with the selected heater, sensors, and filament state; it does not switch among four independent motor drivers.

The printer and tunneled configurations have a [tmc2209 extruder] through [tmc2209 extruder3] section, all with identical settings and all addressing the same driver. Each logical extruder needs one so that it requests the same step-on-both-edges (DEDGE) mode as the others. A tool without one sends single-edge pulses, and the driver, already in DEDGE mode, counts each pulse twice, so that tool extrudes about double. Their configured pins are eBoard PB11 for UART receive, PB10 for UART transmit, address 0, PB14 for step, PB15 for direction, and PB12 for enable. The eBoard uses USART3 for this driver. The host's Creator 5 UART transport and the eBoard's MCU command must both be present; ordinary GPIO UART bitbanging does not implement this hardware path. The configured 0.70 A current approximates stock behavior. The assumed 0.110-ohm sense resistor has been verified working.

Each logical extruder is a separate MCU stepper on the same PB15 direction pin. Stock Klipper toggles a stepper's direction pin relative to that stepper's own last direction, so with four steppers on one pin the actual level ends up as the XOR of all four. A tool then runs backwards whenever an odd number of the other tools last moved in reverse, for example a retract before docking. eBoard builds (CONFIG_C5_EBOARD) therefore write the absolute direction at the start of every move in src/stepper.c. This needs the eBoard reflashed; until then a FIRMWARE_RESTART resets all four to forward.

items.title: Shared MCUs across older printers
items.text:
The MCUs are heavily shared.

Older printers such as the AD5X and AD5M both have the same Nations MCU, but the Gigadevice GD32 chip for the main MCU is completely new, and has not been seen on any other 3D printer made yet. A lot of libraries such as MCLib and addons such as VFA testing are assumed or said to be made by GigaDevice, the MCU manufacturer. In the grape vine, there is supposed to be another printer coming out with the same MCU but as a revision, not a new release.

items.title: Quieter motors
items.text:
Testing

This is in testing on the Kalico phase-stepping branch and needs its mainboard firmware. It isn't in a release yet.

The Creator 5's mainboard drives the X, Y and Z motors itself, through FlashForge's MCLib motor control (see VFA compensation). OpenCreator changes two things in it to make the motors quieter, mostly at printing speeds up to about 100 mm/s:

  • Step interpolation follows the real move between steps.
  • Ripple correction cancels the motors' own wobble, calibrated per motor with the toolhead accelerometer.

items.title: Step interpolation
items.text:
Klipper sends the mainboard a step for each 1/16 of a full step. Between steps the mainboard moves the motor smoothly on to the next one, about 20,000 times a second. Stock guesses when the next step comes by assuming it takes as long as the last one. That is right at a steady speed but wrong whenever the speed changes, so the motor runs ahead or falls behind and then snaps back on the next step. Speed changes are constant in a print: acceleration, input shaping and pressure advance all change it.

On OpenCreator the mainboard's step queue already knows exactly when the next step is due, so the motor is moved on at the real rate. After the last step of a move it stays on that step, instead of running nearly a step past it like stock does.

Nothing changes on the Klipper side: homing, endstops and positions work as before.

items.title: Ripple correction
items.text:
A stepper motor doesn't turn perfectly evenly. Its detent torque and the shape of its current give it a small wobble at fixed multiples of its electrical cycle (four full steps). On the Creator 5 the strong ones are 2, 4, 6 and 8 times per cycle; 4 is once per full step. The wobble shakes the toolhead at those frequencies, so it moves with speed: at 10 mm/s the once-per-step wobble is at 49 Hz, at 20 mm/s at 99 Hz. That is most of the hum you hear at printing speeds.

Ripple correction adds a small opposite current to each motor at those multiples, timed to the motor's position. The right current depends on the speed: for the once-per-step wobble it shrinks as the speed nears the motor's resonance, flips over, and grows again above it. So each multiple has a table of corrections at five speeds, and the mainboard picks the value for the current speed from the step rate. Just above the fastest and below the slowest calibrated speed the correction fades out, as nothing was measured there.

It is calibrated per motor, and per direction of travel, with the toolhead accelerometer.

items.title: Calibrating
items.text:
Dock all the toolheads, then send:

RIPPLE_CALIBRATE

It homes, picks up the first tool and parks in the middle. Then, for each motor, it moves along the diagonal that turns only that motor and measures the vibration at each multiple. It takes about 10 minutes a motor and ends with SAVE_CONFIG. Add AXIS=X or AXIS=Y to do one motor, or SAVE=0 to leave saving for later.

Each speed it tries prints the vibration before and after:

stepper_x harmonic 4 at 297 Hz (60 mm/s motor): forward 565 -> 33, reverse 567 -> 13 mm/s^2

Run it again after changing motors or belts.

items.title: How it finds the correction
items.text:
At one speed, the vibration's strength at a multiple is a simple curve (a quadratic) in the correction's size and timing. Measuring it with no change and with three small test corrections fixes that curve, and the best correction is at its bottom. One more move checks it, and it is only kept if the vibration went down. It does this twice, the second time with smaller test corrections. Both directions are measured on the same out-and-back move.

MCLIB_RIPPLE_MEASURE STEPPER=stepper_x SPEED=30 shows the vibration at each multiple at one speed, and MCLIB_SET_RIPPLE STEPPER=stepper_x shows the saved tables.

items.title: With VFA compensation
items.text: VFA compensation also corrects the 1, 2 and 4 times ripples, but tuned near the frame's resonance, so mostly at higher speeds. The mainboard hands over by speed: where a ripple table covers the motor's current speed, it replaces the VFA value for that ripple; outside the table VFA takes over again, blended in between. Keep both calibrated.

items.title: Fans during calibration
items.text: Calibration holds the mainboard and power supply fans at 50% and waits for them to settle before measuring, like input shaper and VFA calibration do. Otherwise they speed up as the mainboard warms during the test, and their changing vibration throws the measurements off.

items.title: Measured
items.text:
Creator 5 Pro, toolhead accelerometer, board fans held at 50% throughout. The new firmware (step interpolation plus calibrated ripple correction) is the average of three sessions, against the firmware before these changes. Numbers are how much less the toolhead shakes, in three frequency bands: 10–100 / 100–300 / 300–800 Hz. "Diagonal" moves one motor only.

Move Change Y 5 mm/s −24% / −39% / −58% Y 10 mm/s −37% / −38% / −52% Y 20 mm/s −42% / −54% / −45% Y 80 mm/s −4% / −30% / +1% X 5 mm/s −40% / −15% / −17% X 10 mm/s −34% / +18% / −4% X 20 mm/s −23% / −42% / −36% X 40 mm/s +2% / −27% / −4% X 80 mm/s −12% / −22% / −9% X 150 mm/s −11% / −6% / −4% Diagonal 5 mm/s −34% / −29% / −16% Diagonal 20 mm/s −32% / −62% / −14% Diagonal 80 mm/s +2% / −14% / −13% Slow speed changes −2 to −17% / −6 to −10% / −5 to −14%

Repeating the same test 15 minutes apart moves single numbers by up to about ±30%, so read small changes as no change. At the speed each point was calibrated at, the wobble it targets drops by 75 to 95%. The rest of the vibration is the frame and belts, which this doesn't touch; input shaping handles that.

items.title: Inspiration: Prusa's phase stepping
items.text:
This work builds on what Prusa Research published about phase stepping on the Original Prusa XL (firmware 6.0) and later the CORE One. They showed that every stepper motor turns slightly unevenly in its own way, which causes both noise and vertical fine artifacts, and that correcting each motor's drive signal, calibrated by moving the head diagonally at several speeds while recording the toolhead accelerometer, removes most of it. Prusa reported over 96% less motor vibration on the XL. Their help article covers the calibration.

What we took from it: per-motor correction of the motor's own ripple, calibrated with the accelerometer on moves that turn one motor at a time, at several speeds. No Prusa code is used. What differs on the Creator 5:

Prusa phase stepping OpenCreator Motor driver Trinamic stepper drivers The mainboard's own motor control (MCLib), adding a correcting current Steps Replaced: the firmware drives the motor phases from the motion plan (hence the name) Kept: Klipper still sends steps, the mainboard follows the real move between them Correction Per motor and direction Per motor and direction, with a table of corrections per speed Crash detection Turned off while it's on Not affected (skipped step detection is the separate, optional motion guard)

items.title: Why not full phase stepping
items.text: Prusa's phase stepping has the printer's computer send the motor's exact path instead of steps. Step interpolation already follows the path to within a fraction of a 1/16 step, and the measurements show the remaining noise is the motors' wobble, not step size. So OpenCreator does the part that removes it, the ripple correction, without changing how Klipper talks to the mainboard.

items.title: OpenCreator CFW
items.text:
OpenCreator full custom firmware, or CFW, is the deeper Creator 5 integration effort. It aims to make the printer's host software, MCU behavior, toolchanging, and configuration maintainable as one community-developed stack. To gain is more features and more stable software overall compared to stock. CFW is in public alpha; get the latest release. The mostly stock alternative is OpenCreator Legacy.

The work is split between kalico for Klipper and MCU integration (it replaces klipper-c5, which is archived), and opencreator-fs for printer files, configuration, and installation helpers.

items.title: What the newer path aims to support
items.text:
Full custom firmware area Goal Status Base software Maintain Creator 5 stock behavior in a community-developed Klipper host and MCU stack. Finished Installation and updates Provide a tested CFW installation. Finished Tool selection Configure T0 to T3 pickup, docking, and safety in host-side modules and macros. Finished Filament control Integrate AFC standalone for toolchanger filament mapping, loading, and runout handling. Finished ACE Pro Use an ACE Pro as another filament system, each slot feeding its own head, with auto feed and auto load. Finished ACE Pro multiplexing Feed several ACE slots into one head and swap between them. Planned Web and touchscreen Allow for switching filaments on the web. Partial Raspberry Pi host Use USB gadget mode to tunnel Klipper communication from a Raspberry Pi running the Klipper host to the printer. Testing Extend stock features Better VFA testing, stallguard and other similar improvements to software Partial

To see more features that are directly implemented in detail look at CFW Features.

These are goals, and not all of them are finished. The ACE Pro works with auto feed and auto load, multiplexing is in the planning stages, and the Raspberry Pi tunnel is in testing (see OpenCreator for SBC).

Gadget mode Klipper / RPI Klipper is very close to what AnyCubic's modding scene calls Tunneled Vanilla Klipper and a lot of inital insperation was taken to go this route over direct MCU soldering, as it may not be possible on this board, as there has been no direct way (yet) to solder and allow USB passthrough for the MCUs.

items.title: OpenCreator Legacy
items.text: OpenCreator Legacy improves the Creator 5 while retaining its mostly stock FlashForge software and control behavior. It is the path for adding selected modifications without replacing the printer's entire control stack.

items.title: Extend the stock experience
items.text:
Legacy starts with the printer's existing FlashForge software. The Creator-5-Mods repository contains the guides and research, including root access, Loop Script, and Mainsail. The companion Creator-5-Scripts repository contains scripts intended to run on a rooted printer.

Legacy Deprication of Support

Legacy no longer gets meaninful updates and will not get Discord support anymore as CFW has been deemed stable enough to work on most printers. The legacy method still works and will gain version updates to continue to support newer versions of the FlashForge OS Kernel package.

Legacy area Approach Base software Keep the printer's mostly stock FlashForge software and control behavior. (Preserving firmwareExe) Setup Follow individual guides and install only the modifications you want. Root access and scripts Use the documented root and Loop Script paths for printer-side tweaks. Toolchanging Continue using the factory workflow, with any compatible modifications from the guides. Web access Add tools such as Mainsail alongside the stock software. Updates and recovery Check each modification's prerequisite instructions before applying it.

For the newer and supported separate replacement stack, see OpenCreator CFW.

items.title: Plugins
items.text: OpenCreator CFW can install plugins: add-ons that bring their own Klipper modules, macros and Moonraker components without changing OpenCreator's own files. A plugin is a git repository with an opencreator-plugin.json manifest. The example plugin shows each part and is the place to start when making one.

items.title: Using plugins
items.text:
Plugins are managed with oc-plugin over SSH:

Command What it does oc-plugin install <git URL> Download and enable a plugin. --ref <branch or tag> picks a version. oc-plugin list Installed plugins, their version, whether they're enabled, and the git branch and commit. oc-plugin update [id] Pull the newest version of one plugin, or all of them. oc-plugin disable <id> / enable <id> Turn a plugin off or back on without removing it. oc-plugin remove <id> Uninstall it. oc-plugin sync Redo the links and includes; see How it works.

After a change, oc-plugin restarts Klipper and/or Moonraker itself, whichever the plugin needs. It never does that while the printer is printing or paused: it says so, and the change takes effect at the next restart. --no-restart skips the restart.

Plugins installed from a git URL also show up in Fluidd and Mainsail's update manager as oc-plugin-<id>, so they can be updated from there like OpenCreator itself.

To see what's installed without SSH, run the OC_PLUGINS macro, or tap Plugins in GrumpyScreen's macros. It opens a dialog listing every plugin with its version, greyed out if it's disabled and red if its manifest is broken. Tap one for its description, author, what it adds to Klipper and Moonraker, and where it came from. oc-plugin sync rebuilds the list (as config/plugins/_oc-plugins.cfg) every time Klipper starts, so it stays current. Installing, updating and removing still happen over SSH.

items.title: ZMOD plugins
items.text:
oc-plugin install also takes a plugin made for ZMOD, the AD5M/AD5X/C5(P) mod, for example oc-plugin install https://github.com/ghzserg/g28_tenz. Support is basic. A ZMOD plugin has no manifest, just a repo named after the plugin with <name>.cfg (or en/<name>.cfg if it's translated), so oc-plugin takes its id from the repo name and its version from git, and links only that config into Klipper. After that it's listed, updated, disabled and removed like any other plugin.

Its install.sh, uninstall.sh and update.sh are not run, because they expect ZMOD's folders, and Python modules have to be linked by hand, as on ZMOD itself. A plugin whose config uses ZMOD's own macros or settings won't work here as it is. Most plugins are expected to be rewritten.

Plugins run with full access

A plugin's Klipper and Moonraker code runs inside Klipper and Moonraker, with the same access to the printer as they have. Only install plugins you trust. An attacker could gain access to your network via a malicious plugin.

items.title: Making an OpenCreator plugin
items.text:
Copy the example plugin. Its README lists every manifest key. In short:

{
  "id": "hello",
  "name": "Hello OpenCreator",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "klippy_extras": ["klippy/oc_hello.py"],
  "klipper_config": "config/hello.cfg",
  "moonraker_components": ["moonraker/oc_hello.py"],
  "moonraker_config": "moonraker/hello.conf"
}
  • klippy_extras: Klippy modules, the same as a file in klippy/extras. A module is loaded by the config section of the same name, so oc_hello.py is loaded by [oc_hello].
  • klipper_config: one Klipper config file, with your module's section and macros. It's included after the rest of printer.cfg, so it can add to OpenCreator's sections.
  • moonraker_components and moonraker_config: the same, for Moonraker.

Module names must be unique. A plugin whose module has the same name as one of Kalico's, or as another plugin's, is refused and isn't installed. Give yours a prefix.

To try a plugin while writing it, install the folder straight from disk: oc-plugin install /usr/data/my-plugin. That's a copy, so install it again after each change, and it isn't offered in the update manager.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Plugins are kept in /usr/data/opencreator/plugins/<id> (a git checkout). Nothing from a plugin is copied into Kalico or Moonraker. oc-plugin sync links it in:

Plugin part Where it goes klippy_extras Symlinked into Kalico's klippy/plugins/ (Klipper without that folder: klippy/extras/) klipper_config Symlinked as plugins/<id>.cfg next to printer.cfg, which includes [include plugins/*.cfg] moonraker_components Symlinked into Moonraker's moonraker/components/ moonraker_config Copied, with the plugin's [update_manager] section, to plugins/moonraker/<id>.conf, included by moonraker.conf with [include plugins/moonraker/*.conf]

Kalico's klippy/plugins/ is git-ignored, so Kalico updates leave plugin links alone. Kalico also refuses to start if a module there has the name of one of its own.

oc-plugin only removes or replaces links that point into the plugins folder. A file it didn't make is never touched. If something is in its way, it reports that and the plugin isn't installed. The two include lines are added to printer.cfg and moonraker.conf once, if they're missing. In printer.cfg the line goes before the SAVE_CONFIG block. plugins/moonraker/00-oc-plugins.conf only holds a comment. It's there because Moonraker, unlike Klipper, refuses an include that matches no files.

On the printer, 10-klipper.sh runs oc-plugin sync --only klipper before every Klippy start, and 20-msmr.sh runs oc-plugin sync --only moonraker before every Moonraker start. This is why an update from Fluidd, which only does a git pull and restarts, still links any file the new version added. oc-plugin itself lives in /usr/data/opencreator/plugin-manager/, which the installer and the OpenCreator updater keep up to date. 10-klipper.sh links it into /opt/bin.

items.title: Tunneled and SBC installs
items.text: oc-plugin also works on a Raspberry Pi running Klipper. There, the default folders are ~/opencreator-plugins, ~/klipper, ~/printer_data/config and ~/moonraker. Nothing runs sync at each start there, so run oc-plugin sync after updating a plugin from the update manager. To use other folders, set OC_PLUGINS_DIR, OC_KLIPPER_DIR, OC_CONFIG_DIR and OC_MOONRAKER_DIR, plus OC_MOONRAKER_URL for the restarts.

items.title: Current print workflow
items.text:
The C5_PRINT_START macro prepares only the tools the job uses. This page describes the current config; not every printer and filament combination has been tested.

The slicer or print dispatcher supplies TOOL=0..3, HOTEND, and BED. TOOLS=0,3, for example, identifies all tools used by a multi-tool job; TOOL must be in that list. HOTEND0 through HOTEND3 can override the shared hotend temperature for individual tools. The macro checks the physical filament-presence input for each used tool. A missing tool's filament cancels the job; unused tools are not required to be loaded.

When a file has no C5_PRINT_START line, the print dispatcher (virtual_sdcard.py) builds one from the first 64 KB and the last 64 KB of the file:

  • TOOL is the first T0–T3. If the file has none, it's the first slot with filament used.
  • HOTEND is the first M109, else the first M104. If neither exists, it's that tool's nozzle_temperature_initial_layer from Orca's config block. Orca leaves out the heating line in single-tool T0 jobs.
  • BED is the first M140 or M190.

If no hotend temperature can be found, the job stops before any motion, and the reason is printed to the console.

items.title: Preparation order
items.text:
flowchart TD
  A[Check filament in every used tool] -->|missing| X[Cancel the job]
  A --> C[Start preheating tools<br/>to max 100 °C & bed to temp]
  C --> B[Home, then wait for the bed]
  B --> D{Flow calibration<br/>or purge on?}
  D -->|yes| E[For each used tool:<br/>pick up, nozzle Z, heat,<br/>flow / purge, cool, dock]
  D -->|no| W
  E --> W[Wait for used tools<br/>to reach their preheat]
  W --> F{Bed leveling on?}
  F -->|yes| G[Adaptive mesh]
  F -->|no| H[Load saved mesh]
  G --> I[Pick up first tool, apply nozzle Z,<br/>park, other tools to idle temperature,<br/>wait for print temperature]
  H --> I
  I --> J{Purge on?}
  J -->|yes| M[KAMP purge line<br/>in front of the objects]
  J -->|no| O
  M --> O[Slicer G-code starts]
  1. Start a non-blocking preheat of every used tool to at most 100 °C, so the tools warm while the printer homes and the bed heats.
  2. Home for printing. If a tool is attached, the Creator 5 homing helper handles its docking before Z homing. Then wait for the bed to reach its target.
  3. If flow calibration or purge is enabled, prepare each used tool in turn: select it, establish its nozzle Z reference, heat it to its material temperature, run the selected flow and/or purge operation, cool it for docking, and release it.
  4. Wait for every used tool to reach its preheat (re-applied, since docking after priming may have left it cooler). Then clear the old mesh. When bed leveling is enabled, create an adaptive mesh. Otherwise, load the saved default mesh if one exists.
  5. Probe the bed center as a check, then select the job's initial tool. Apply its automatic nozzle Z, verify that a safe nozzle Z is available, smart park, and wait for its print temperature. The print's other tools are set to their slicer idle temperature (Orca's Idle temperature), or 100 °C if it has none.
  6. If purge is enabled, draw KAMP's purge line (LINE_PURGE) just in front of the printed objects. The slicer's print moves follow.

With purge_line_all_tools on, the print's other tools (TOOLS and the slicer's used tools) each draw a purge line too, after the mesh and before the initial tool is picked up. Each one is picked up, heated to its own first-layer temperature, draws its line further out than the last (purge_tool_spacing in KAMP_Settings.cfg, 8 mm by default), then cools and docks like after priming. The initial tool's line is drawn last, nearest the objects. A tool's line is left out, with a message, if there's no room for it in front of or left of the objects, or the file has no object outlines (Orca's Label objects).

The center probe check does not itself replace the automatic nozzle Z measurement. A missing safe nozzle Z is a print-stopping condition, not a reason to continue at zero offset.

Flow calibration, purge, the purge line and bed leveling can be toggled in the printer's Misc controls or overridden for a job with FLOW_CALIBRATION=0|1, PURGE=0|1, PURGE_LINE=0|1 and BED_LEVELING=0|1 (see How to toggle features). Turning off flow and purge removes those preparation operations; it does not bypass the filament-presence or nozzle-Z safety checks. See Printer features for how the flow measurement works.

At a normal job end, C5_PRINT_STOP handles tool parking and heater shutdown. The optional lower-bed-at-end setting is separate from print-start bed leveling. The printer configuration also routes cancellation through the stop sequence, but a shutdown can prevent ordinary G-code cleanup. Confirm the machine state before resuming after an MCU fault.
